skills.title: Classify natural resources as renewable or non-renewable and as biotic or abiotic
Read where resources are found on a map and explain why some are found everywhere (ubiquitous) and others only in some places (localised)
Trace cause-effect chains from overuse of a resource to depletion or pollution
Judge whether a use of a resource is sustainable, including how communities can manage shared resources (commons)

expectations: Natural resources are materials and energy from nature that people use to meet their needs, such as air, water, soil, forests, minerals and sunlight.
Renewable resources (sunlight, wind, water, forests, fish) are replenished by nature within a human lifetime, but they can still be used up or spoiled if used faster than they renew.
Non-renewable resources such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and metal ores took millions of years to form and exist in limited amounts.
Biotic resources come from living things (forests, animals, fish); abiotic resources come from non-living things (water, soil, rocks, minerals, air).
Resources are unevenly distributed: some are found almost everywhere (air), others only in certain places (coal is concentrated in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh).
Overuse causes depletion and pollution, for example falling groundwater where pumping is faster than rain can refill it.
Sustainable use meets today's needs without harming future generations: reduce, reuse, recycle, conserve, and let communities share rules for commons like ponds, grazing land and forests.

skills.title: Order the main dynasties and events of the 13th-17th centuries on a timeline and name the century of a year
Read historical maps to describe how kingdoms' territories changed over time
Explain causes and effects of political changes such as expansion, decline and resistance
Interpret historical sources and recognise that different sources carry different viewpoints
Identify regional powers and resistance that existed alongside the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals

expectations: The Delhi Sultanate (from 1206) was ruled in turn by five dynasties, Mamluk (Slave), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, until 1526.

In 1526 Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat and began Mughal rule; Akbar (ruled 1556-1605) expanded and organised the empire, and it reached its largest size under Aurangzeb (died 1707), who also faced many revolts.

Many other powers existed at the same time, such as the Vijayanagara Empire (founded 1336), the Bahmani and later Deccan sultanates, Rajput kingdoms, the Ahoms of Assam and Gondwana; no single ruler controlled all of India for the whole period.

Rulers expanded through war, alliances, revenue systems and administration, and they were resisted, for example by Maharana Pratap at Haldighati (1576), Rani Durgavati (1564), Lachit Borphukan at Saraighat (1671) and the Sikh Gurus.
Conquest brought violence, including raids, destruction of cities and places of worship, and heavy taxes, along with new systems of administration, building and cultural exchange.
Historians compare many sources (court chronicles, inscriptions, coins, travellers' accounts) because each has its own viewpoint.
The 13th century means the years 1201-1300; the 17th century means 1601-1700.

expectations: European traders came for spices and textiles: the Portuguese (Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498), then the Dutch, the English East India Company (chartered in 1600) and the French.

The Company built forts and its own armies of Indian soldiers (sepoys) under British officers, took sides in local disputes and won key battles at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764); in 1765 it got the diwani, the right to collect revenue, of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
It expanded through wars, subsidiary alliances and annexations (such as under the Doctrine of Lapse); after the revolt of 1857, the British Crown took direct control in 1858.

Heavy land revenue (for example under the Permanent Settlement of 1793) burdened peasants; cheap British machine-made cloth ruined many Indian weavers; farmers were pushed to grow cash crops like indigo; famines such as Bengal 1770 killed millions; and wealth flowed to Britain, which Dadabhai Naoroji called the 'drain of wealth'.
Railways, telegraph and ports were built mainly to serve colonial needs, moving raw materials, goods and troops, though Indians also came to use them.
Indians resisted in many ways: peasant and tribal revolts, the indigo revolt (1859-60), the revolt of 1857, and Champaran (1917).

expectations: Universal adult franchise means every adult citizen has the right to vote, whatever their religion, caste, gender, wealth or education, and every vote has equal value.
In India a citizen who is 18 or older and registered on the electoral roll can vote (Article 326); the age was lowered from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment in 1988.

India gave the vote to all adults from its very first general election (1951-52), while some older democracies took much longer to include women, for example the UK (equal voting age only in 1928) and Switzerland (1971 for national elections).

The Election Commission of India (Article 324, set up on 25 January 1950) is independent and conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President, and enforces the Model Code of Conduct; State Election Commissions run panchayat and municipal elections.
Voting is secret; EVMs record votes and the VVPAT shows a paper slip so the voter can verify; indelible ink prevents voting twice; NOTA lets a voter reject all candidates.
Lok Sabha elections use first-past-the-post: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without more than half the votes.
Democracy is more than voting: it also needs free speech, rights, a free press, courts and citizens holding leaders accountable between elections.

expectations: India's Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).

Lok Sabha members are directly elected by the people from 543 constituencies for up to five years; most Rajya Sabha members are elected by the elected members of state and some union territory legislative assemblies for six-year terms, with one-third retiring every two years, and 12 are nominated by the President.
A bill is introduced, debated and passed in both Houses and becomes a law only after the President gives assent; a money bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.

The party or alliance with a majority in the Lok Sabha (at least 272 of 543) forms the government: the President appoints its leader as Prime Minister, and other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and must keep its confidence; if a no-confidence motion passes, the government must resign.
Parliament checks the government through Question Hour, Zero Hour, debates, committees and control over money (the budget).
The political executive (ministers) is elected and changes with elections; the permanent executive (civil servants such as IAS officers) carries out policies and continues.

expectations: Producing any good or service needs four factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Land means all natural resources used in production, such as ground, water, minerals and forests, not only soil.
Labour is human effort, both physical and mental: a farmer, a mason, a teacher and a software engineer all provide labour.

expectations: The Earth has seven continents (Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia) and five oceans (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic); Asia is the largest continent and the Pacific the largest ocean.

Major physical features include mountain ranges (Himalayas, Andes, Rockies, Alps), great rivers (Nile, Amazon, Yangtze, Mississippi) and deserts (Sahara, Gobi, Atacama, and Antarctica, the largest, a cold desert).

Climate depends on latitude (hotter near the Equator, colder near the poles), altitude, distance from the sea and winds; the Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons because of the tilt of the Earth's axis.
Natural vegetation and ways of life follow climate: rainforests in the equatorial Amazon and Congo basins, grasslands in temperate interiors, tundra near the Arctic.
Flat maps distort sizes: on Mercator-style maps lands near the poles, such as Greenland, look much bigger than they are (Africa is about 14 times larger than Greenland).

India is linked to the world by sea routes across the Indian Ocean (through the Strait of Malacca to the east and the Suez Canal to Europe), by trade and supply chains (parts of a phone come from many countries), and by people of Indian origin living abroad.

skills.title: Order the main phases and events of the freedom struggle (1857-1947) on a timeline

expectations: Resistance to British rule took many forms over a long time, from the revolt of 1857 and tribal and peasant uprisings to organised national movements.

The Indian National Congress (founded 1885) began with moderates such as Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale who used petitions and reasoned criticism; assertive leaders such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal demanded swaraj and led Swadeshi and boycott after the Partition of Bengal (1905).

Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915, led satyagrahas at Champaran (1917), Kheda and Ahmedabad (1918), then mass movements: Non-Cooperation (1920-22), Civil Disobedience with the Dandi Salt March (1930), and Quit India (1942).
Events like the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) brought many more people into the struggle; Non-Cooperation was called off after the violence at Chauri Chaura (1922).

Revolutionaries such as Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad, and Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army, took other paths; women, workers, peasants, students and tribal communities all took part.
India became independent on 15 August 1947, together with the partition of the country, which caused great violence and displacement.

skills.title: Identify the main features of the Nagara, Dravida and Vesara temple styles and match them to regions

expectations: Nagara temples, found mostly in north India, have a curving tower (shikhara) rising above the sanctum (garbhagriha), for example the Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho.

Dravida temples, found in south India, have a stepped, pyramid-like tower (vimana) over the sanctum and, in later temples, tall gateway towers (gopurams) in the outer walls, for example the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur, completed around 1010 CE under Rajaraja Chola I.
Vesara temples mix features of both and are found in the Deccan, for example under the later Chalukyas and the Hoysalas.
Stupas such as the Great Stupa at Sanchi have a dome (anda), a railing (vedika), a small square enclosure on top (harmika), an umbrella (chhatra) and carved gateways (toranas).
Rock-cut architecture was carved out of solid rock: the Ajanta caves, the Kailasa temple at Ellora (8th century, carved downward out of a single rock) and the rathas of Mahabalipuram.

Earlier Indian buildings mostly used post-and-lintel construction (pillars and beams); true arches and domes became widespread from the 13th century in Indo-Islamic buildings such as the Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal, which also used minarets, calligraphy and charbagh gardens.
Buildings are evidence of the technology, beliefs, rulers, trade and artisans of their time; texts such as the Shilpa Shastras guided builders.

expectations: India has a single integrated judiciary: subordinate courts at the district level, a High Court for each state or group of states, and the Supreme Court at the top (set up in 1950 in New Delhi).
A person who is not satisfied with a lower court's decision can usually appeal to a higher court.

Civil cases are disputes about property, money, contracts, rent or family matters, filed by the affected person; criminal cases are offences such as theft or assault, where an FIR is lodged with the police, the state prosecutes, and punishment can follow.

Courts settle disputes, interpret the Constitution, and can strike down laws or government actions that violate it (judicial review); they protect Fundamental Rights through writs (Article 32 in the Supreme Court, Article 226 in High Courts).

The judiciary is independent of the government: judges can be removed only by a special process in Parliament (impeachment) for proven misbehaviour or incapacity, and their salaries cannot be cut to punish them.

Justice must be reachable for all: free legal aid for those who cannot afford a lawyer, Lok Adalats for quick settlement by agreement, and Public Interest Litigation (PIL) so that anyone can approach the court on behalf of people whose rights are violated.

expectations: A citizen is a full member of a country with rights and duties; India has a single citizenship for the whole country, and citizenship can be acquired by birth, descent, registration or naturalisation under the Citizenship Act, 1955.

The Constitution guarantees six Fundamental Rights: the Right to Equality, the Right to Freedom, the Right against Exploitation, the Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies.

Some Fundamental Rights protect every person in India, citizen or not (equality before law, Article 14; life and personal liberty, Article 21), while some belong only to citizens (the freedoms of Article 19, and Articles 15 and 16).
Rights are not unlimited: the Constitution allows reasonable restrictions for public order, security, decency, health and the rights of others.
Article 32 lets a person go directly to the Supreme Court if Fundamental Rights are violated; Dr B. R. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution.

The Fundamental Duties (Article 51A, added in 1976, now eleven) include respecting the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem, promoting harmony, protecting the environment, developing a scientific temper, safeguarding public property, and the duty of parents to give children aged 6-14 opportunities for education.
Rights and duties are linked: one person's right is another person's duty, and duties keep everyone's rights safe.

items.answer: Any two of: by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalisation.

registration, naturalisation

Prompt: by ___ and by ___

verified.solverAnswer: Any two: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation.

items.prompt_en: Predict: a man plays a loudspeaker at full volume at 2 a.m. every night and says it is his freedom of expression. What would a court be likely to say?
items.prompt_hi: Socho: ek aadmi har raat 2 baje full volume mein loudspeaker bajaata hai aur kehta hai ki yeh uski abhivyakti ki azaadi hai. Court kya kahega?
items.answer: That freedoms have reasonable restrictions; loud noise at night harms other people's health and right to live in peace (part of the right to life), so it can be stopped. Courts have upheld limits on loudspeakers at night.
acceptable: reasonable restrictions; others' right to peace
doosron ke haq ka dhyan; raat mein mana
hints: Ask how the neighbours are affected
Point: freedom ends where it harms others' rights
Prompt: the court will say rights have ___
Assert: reasonable restrictions protect others' rights

verified.solverAnswer: Freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions; others' right to peace/health prevails; it can be stopped.

items.prompt_en: Contrast an Indian citizen and a foreign tourist in India: which Fundamental Rights do both have, and which are for citizens only?
items.prompt_hi: Ek Indian naagrik aur India mein ek videshi tourist ka contrast karo: kaunse Mool Adhikaar dono ke paas hain, aur kaunse sirf naagrikon ke?
items.answer: Both: equality before law (Article 14), life and personal liberty (Article 21), freedom of religion (Article 25). Citizens only: the freedoms of Article 19 (speech, movement, residence, profession), protection from discrimination (Article 15) and equal opportunity in public jobs (Article 16); voting is also only for citizens.
acceptable: both have 14 and 21; only citizens have Article 19 freedoms
hints: Ask whether a tourist can be jailed without a fair process
Point: Article 19 freedoms are for citizens
Prompt: both = ___; citizens only = ___
Assert: some rights protect every person, some only citizens

verified.solverAnswer: Both: Articles 14, 20, 21, 25; citizens only: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29-30.

items.prompt_en: A student says: 'Fundamental Duties are only for the government; citizens only have rights.' What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Ek student kehta hai: 'Mool Kartavya sirf sarkaar ke liye hain; naagrikon ke sirf adhikaar hain.' Kya galat hai?
items.answer: Fundamental Duties in Article 51A are duties of every citizen, such as respecting the Constitution and the flag, protecting the environment, safeguarding public property and promoting harmony.
acceptable: duties are for every citizen
har naagrik ke kartavya
hints: Ask who Article 51A is addressed to
Point: 'It shall be the duty of every citizen…'
Prompt: duties are for every ___
Assert: Fundamental Duties belong to every citizen

verified.solverAnswer: Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A) are duties of every citizen.

items.prompt_en: Why did Dr B. R. Ambedkar call the Right to Constitutional Remedies the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
items.prompt_hi: Dr B. R. Ambedkar ne Samvaidhanik Upchaaron ke Adhikaar ko Samvidhaan ka 'hriday aur aatma' kyon kaha?
items.answer: Because without a way to enforce them, the other rights would be only words on paper; Article 32 lets anyone whose Fundamental Rights are violated go directly to the Supreme Court.
acceptable: it makes all other rights enforceable
baaki adhikaar isi se laagu hote hain
hints: Ask what happens if a right is broken and nobody can stop it
Point: Article 32 opens the Supreme Court's door
Prompt: without remedies, rights would be only ___
Assert: it makes every other right enforceable

verified.solverAnswer: Without a remedy to enforce them, rights would be empty; Article 32 gives direct access to the Supreme Court.

items.prompt_en: After a festival, some people break the benches and lights in a public park. Which Fundamental Duty does this go against, and what should citizens do?
items.prompt_hi: Ek tyohaar ke baad kuch log public park ki benches aur lights tod dete hain. Yeh kis Mool Kartavya ke khilaaf hai, aur naagrikon ko kya karna chahiye?
items.answer: The duty to safeguard public property and to abjure violence; citizens should not damage it, should report damage to the local authority, and can help look after shared spaces.
acceptable: safeguard public property
saarvajanik sampatti ki raksha
hints: Ask who paid for the park benches
Point: public property belongs to all of us
Prompt: the duty to ___ public property
Assert: safeguarding public property is every citizen's duty

verified.solverAnswer: Duty to safeguard public property and abjure violence; don't damage, report, help maintain.

items.prompt_en: Make a two-column chart in words, right on the left and matching duty on the right, and fill in: right to education → ?; right to a clean, healthy environment → ?; freedom of religion → ?
items.prompt_hi: Shabdon mein do column ka chart banao, baayein adhikaar aur daayein uska kartavya, aur bharo: shiksha ka adhikaar → ?; saaf, swasth mahaul ka adhikaar → ?; dharm ki azaadi → ?
items.answer: Education → parents and guardians' duty to give their child (6-14) opportunities for education; clean environment → the duty to protect and improve the natural environment; freedom of religion → the duty to promote harmony and respect for all.
acceptable: parents educate; protect environment; promote harmony
hints: Ask who must send a child to school
Point: duties match rights like two halves
Prompt: education ↔ ___; environment ↔ ___; religion ↔ ___
Assert: each right is safeguarded by a matching duty

verified.solverAnswer: Education -> parents' duty to provide education (6-14); environment -> protect and improve natural environment; religion -> promote harmony and respect.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend, with an example, why 'my rights' and 'my duties' are two sides of the same coin.
items.prompt_hi: Ek dost ko udaharan dekar samjhao ki 'mere adhikaar' aur 'mere kartavya' ek hi sikke ke do pehlu kyon hain.
items.answer: My right is safe only when others do their duty, and their rights are safe when I do mine; for example, my right to be heard needs others to listen without shouting me down, and my freedom of speech comes with the duty not to spread lies or hatred against others.
acceptable: rights need others' duties, with an example
hints: Ask them to pick one right first

Assert: rights and duties protect each other

skills.title: Calculate and interpret population density
Explain why population is unevenly distributed, using physical and human factors and a density map
Explain how population changes through births, deaths and migration, and compute simple changes
Read population composition (sex ratio, age structure, literacy) and explain population as a resource (demographic dividend)

expectations: Population density = number of people ÷ area, in persons per km²; India's density in Census 2011 was 382 per km².

Population is unevenly distributed: fertile plains with water (the Ganga plains), coasts and cities are dense, while high mountains, deserts, thick forests and very cold areas are sparse (in 2011, Bihar had about 1,106 per km² and Arunachal Pradesh about 17).
Population changes through births, deaths and migration: change = births − deaths + people moving in − people moving out.
India's population was about 121 crore (1.21 billion) in Census 2011, and by UN estimates India became the world's most populous country around 2023.
Composition describes a population by age, sex, literacy, rural or urban residence and occupation; the sex ratio is the number of females per 1,000 males (943 in India in 2011).
People are a resource: a large working-age population can be a 'demographic dividend' if people are healthy, educated, skilled and employed.

skills.title: Classify a settlement as urban or rural using the official criteria (statutory towns and census towns)
Trace the long history of Indian cities on a timeline, from Harappan cities to planned modern cities
Explain the causes of urbanisation (push and pull factors) and the challenges it brings
Evaluate solutions and the role of urban local bodies in managing cities

expectations: In India an urban area is either a statutory town (with a municipal corporation, municipality, cantonment board or notified town area) or a census town (population at least 5,000, density at least 400 per km², and at least 75% of male main workers in non-farm work).
About 31% of India's people (around 37.7 crore) lived in urban areas in Census 2011, and the share has been rising (about 17% in 1951).

Indian cities have a very long history: planned Harappan cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira (from about 2600 BCE), ancient capitals such as Pataliputra, medieval cities such as Vijayanagara and Fatehpur Sikri, colonial port cities such as Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, and planned cities after independence such as Chandigarh.
People move to cities because of pull factors (jobs, education, health care, services) and push factors in villages (low farm incomes, lack of work or services).
Fast growth brings challenges: housing shortages and slums, traffic, air and water pollution, waste, water scarcity, urban flooding and heat.

Urban local bodies (municipal corporations, municipalities, nagar panchayats), given constitutional status by the 74th Amendment (1992), plan and provide services; good planning, public transport, waste segregation, rainwater harvesting and protecting lakes and wetlands help.

Bhakti stressed personal, loving devotion to God, either with form (saguna, such as Rama or Krishna) or without form (nirguna), and simple worship over elaborate ritual; many saints questioned social barriers and taught that all devotees are equal.

Sufis, Islamic mystics such as Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti in Ajmer and Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi, taught love of God, compassion and service, lived in khanqahs, and used music (sama, qawwali) in devotion.

Saints and poets composed in the languages people spoke, so regional literatures grew richer: Marathi, Hindavi, Braj, Awadhi, Bengali, Assamese, Kannada, Punjabi; Amir Khusrau wrote in both Persian and Hindavi.

Music and painting flourished too: the Hindustani and Carnatic traditions developed (Tansen at Akbar's court; Purandara Dasa in the south), along with miniature painting at Mughal, Rajput and Deccan courts.
The Bhakti tradition began much earlier in the Tamil region with the Alvars and Nayanars (around the 6th-9th centuries) and grew in different regions at different times.
